header: Small, fast limiters (pure, no I/O): a sliding window of the last N requests per key, and a failure lock (too many wrong passwords in a while locks the key for a while). Both are O(1) per call and bounded in memory (a key table that grows past MAX_KEYS drops its expired and then its oldest keys), so they cost the request nothing worth measuring. The honest limit: the tables live in the memory of one server copy. On Vercel a burst can be served by several copies, each with its own table, so the real ceiling for a determined caller is (the limit x the copies that answer). That still stops a script from one machine at full speed and the casual guessing; a limit shared by every copy would need a store they all reach (the database). Who is calling: I use the login's ticket as the key when there is one, else the address Vercel puts in x-forwarded-for (Vercel overwrites a value the caller sends).

symbols.name: createLimiter
symbols.sig: export function createLimiter(opts: { max: number; windowMs: number })
doc: I allow at most `max` calls per `windowMs` for each key

symbols.name: createFailureLock
symbols.sig: export function createFailureLock(opts: { max: number; windowMs: number })
doc: My rule: `max` failures within `windowMs` lock the key until the oldest of them is `windowMs` old; a success clears the key

symbols.name: clientIp
symbols.sig: export function clientIp(headers: { get(name: string): string | null }): string
doc: I take the caller's address from x-forwarded-for, which Vercel sets (its first entry is the client) and overwrites over what the caller sent; "unknown" when there is none
